items.lessonTitle: Adi Parva: the snake sacrifice frame

neighbors.heading: the glory of letting it pass
neighbors.text: Today a sage sat with a dead snake on his shoulders and called forgiveness a sage's strength, while his son's curse started a chain. Jewish wisdom says it too. A proverb sings: "it is his glory to pass over a transgression." And the rabbis taught that whoever lets a wrong go, Heaven lets their own wrongs go too.
neighbors.difference: In the epic, forgiveness is a sage's power, a strength his discipline has earned. In Jewish teaching it's also a mirror: as you pass over other people's wrongs, God passes over yours.
neighbors.shared: a chain of hurt can stop with one person who lets go.

neighbors.heading: hatred doesn't end hatred
neighbors.text: Today one insult became a curse, and the curse became a death: a chain, link by link. Buddhists name the way out. The Dhammapada says: "hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule." Shamika made the same quiet move. He wouldn't add a link.
neighbors.difference: In the epic the curse, once spoken, runs its course, and the story follows the chain to Janamejaya's fire. The Buddha teaches that each link is fed in our own minds, so it can be loosened from the inside.
neighbors.shared: you can be the place where a chain of anger ends.

neighbors.heading: God as your witness
neighbors.text: Today a prince spoke his vow before elders, so he couldn't take it back. Muslims treat a sworn word as weighty too. One chapter of the Qur'an opens: "O ye who believe! Fulfil your undertakings." Another verse warns against breaking an oath once you've made God your surety, the witness to what you promised.
neighbors.difference: Bhishma's witnesses are human elders, and his vow gives away a throne. In Islam the first witness is God, and the Qur'an sets a way to make amends for a broken oath, such as feeding the poor.
neighbors.shared: a promise said out loud is a gift to everyone who heard it.

neighbors.heading: the animal that makes promises
neighbors.text: Today a prince chose to speak his vow before elders, on purpose, so it would hold. Philosophers have marveled at that power. Friedrich Nietzsche called the human being the animal able to make promises: we bind our future selves with words, and other people build their lives on them. Keeping one, he thought, takes a long memory and a steady will.
neighbors.difference: Bhishma's vow belongs to dharma, sealed before elders and honored by the gods in the story. For Nietzsche, a promise is a human achievement, made of memory and will, with no heaven needed to seal it.
neighbors.shared: a promise is how you hand your future self to someone else.
neighbors.sources: Friedrich Nietzsche, On the Genealogy of Morals, second essay, section 1 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: higher still: truthful living
neighbors.text: Today Bhishma said the earth could lose its scent before he would give up truth. Sikhs hold truth that high, and then one step higher. Guru Nanak taught that truth is above everything, and higher still is truthful living. For the Guru, truth isn't only a word kept once; it's a way of living, every day.
neighbors.difference: Bhishma's truth is a vow never to marry or rule. The Gurus taught truthful living inside ordinary life: marrying, working honestly, raising a family and sharing. Two pictures of keeping faith with truth.
neighbors.shared: a life can be the proof of what a person says.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Sri Raag, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: let yes be yes
neighbors.text: Today Bhishma would not break his word, even when the woman it was made for asked him to. Jesus spoke about words that hold. "But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay," he says in the Sermon on the Mount. A yes should simply mean yes, with nothing extra needed to prop it up.
neighbors.difference: Bhishma's whole life rests on one great sworn vow. In the same passage Jesus says "Swear not at all," asking for speech so plain that no oath is needed. Christians differ on oaths today; many churches allow them, while Quakers and some others decline them.
neighbors.shared: a word you keep becomes a place others can stand.

neighbors.heading: joy at someone else's good
neighbors.text: Today a boy watched his stronger cousin, and the story says jealousy took hold, until it became poison in the food. Buddhists practice an antidote. Mudita means gladness at another's good fortune, one of four boundless states the Buddha taught, beside loving-kindness, compassion and equanimity. It's grown on purpose, often starting with a dear friend's win.
neighbors.difference: The epic shows envy growing and lets us watch where it leads. Buddhist practice works on it ahead of time, training the mind toward gladness until another's success stops feeling like your loss.
neighbors.shared: a cousin's win doesn't have to be your loss.
neighbors.sources: Digha Nikaya 13, Tevijja Sutta, the four boundless states (Rhys Davids; paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: brothers and envy
neighbors.text: Today a grudge started young, between cousins raised in one palace. Catholics know an old telling of it: Cain and Abel. The Catechism calls envy a capital sin, sadness at another's good, and Scripture says: "But by the envy of the devil, death came into the world." The cure it names is goodwill: learning to be glad for the other.
neighbors.difference: The epic weighs both boys: Bhima's rough play and Duryodhana's jealousy. Catholic teaching treats envy as a sin of one's own heart, to be confessed and healed by God's grace, whatever the other person did.
neighbors.shared: a family grudge is easier to heal while it's still small.
neighbors.sources: Wisdom 2:24 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2538–2540 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: drawn out of the water
neighbors.text: Today a basket floated down to a couple with no child, and a boy found a home. Jews tell a story with the same river in it. Moses, laid in an ark of bulrushes, is lifted from the Nile by Pharaoh's daughter, and Exodus says simply: "he became her son." She named him for it: "Because I drew him out of the water."
neighbors.difference: Moses's own mother is brought in to nurse him, and he grows up knowing his people. Karna learns whose son he is only on the eve of war. Moses's story leads to a people's freedom; Karna's, to one man's divided heart.
neighbors.shared: the one who takes you in is family too.

neighbors.heading: through you, not from you
neighbors.text: Today one mother let go upstream and another took the baby in downstream, and he carried both into his life. The poet Kahlil Gibran wrote of children: "They come through you but not from you, And though they are with you yet they belong not to you." No child is only the story of the people who made or raised them.
neighbors.difference: Gibran loosens every claim: children belong to Life itself, not to any parent. The epic weighs both claims: Kunti's blood and Radha's care each shape Karna, and he is called Radheya, after the woman who raised him.
neighbors.shared: every child is bigger than any one parent's story.

neighbors.heading: the left hand doesn't know
neighbors.text: Today Vidura saved a family with a riddle, a digger and a boat, and never once stood in the light. Jesus praised help like that. "But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth," he says, "That thine alms may be in secret." Quiet good, he teaches, is seen by God.
neighbors.difference: Vidura hides his help to keep the Pandavas alive in a court that wants them dead. Jesus asks for hidden giving so that the good is done for God, not for praise.
neighbors.shared: the best help often arrives without a name on it.

neighbors.heading: help given in secret
neighbors.text: Today Vidura's help came hidden: a riddle, a tunnel, a boatman with the right words. Muslims prize hidden help too. The Qur'an says giving openly is good, but giving in secret to people in need is better. And a hadith counts among the people God shelters someone who gives so quietly the left hand doesn't know what the right gave.
neighbors.difference: Vidura's secrecy is a shield against a dangerous court. In Islam, secret giving guards the giver's heart against showing off, so the gift is for God alone.
neighbors.shared: quiet kindness still reaches the far bank.

neighbors.heading: the open kitchen
neighbors.text: Today Yudhishthira fed a great crowd before he set foot in his new hall. Sikhs keep a kitchen at the heart of the gurdwara. Langar, the free community meal, goes back to Guru Nanak, and tradition says Guru Amar Das asked every visitor, even an emperor, to sit and eat in it first. Everyone sits together in rows and eats the same food.
neighbors.difference: Yudhishthira's feast honors brahmanas as a royal rite, blessing a new beginning. Langar is an ongoing open table for anyone of any faith or none, cooked and served by volunteers.
neighbors.shared: a place becomes holy when people are fed there.
neighbors.sources: Sikh tradition of langar, from Guru Nanak and Guru Amar Das (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: I was hungry
neighbors.text: Today a new hall was opened by feeding people first, with music and gifts. Catholics count feeding the hungry among the works of mercy. Jesus, describing the last judgment, says: "I was hungry, and you gave me to eat." In his telling, whoever feeds the least of his brothers and sisters has fed him.
neighbors.difference: Yudhishthira feeds people as a rite to begin something new and auspicious. For Catholics, feeding the hungry is a daily work of mercy, and Christ himself is met in the hungry person.
neighbors.shared: the best way to open a new home is to feed someone.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 25:35 (Douay-Rheims) · Matthew 25:40 (paraphrase) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 2447 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: get yourself a teacher
neighbors.text: Today everyone told Yudhishthira yes, and he still sent for the one friend who would tell him the truth. The rabbis gave similar advice. Pirkei Avot teaches: make for yourself a teacher, and acquire a friend. Proverbs adds: "in the multitude of counsellors there is safety." Many Jews still study in chavruta, with partners who push back.
neighbors.difference: Yudhishthira seeks out one person who sees further, Krishna, whom many Hindus worship as God. In Jewish learning the teacher is human, and study partners are meant to question each other, not only defer.
neighbors.shared: the best counsel comes from someone who won't just flatter you.

neighbors.heading: the whole of the path
neighbors.text: Today a king set aside a room full of yes and sent for a friend who would tell him the truth. Buddhists tell of Ananda saying that good friendship is half the holy life. The Buddha corrected him: not half. Admirable friendship, he said, is the whole of the holy life.
neighbors.difference: Yudhishthira turns to Krishna, a friend whom many Hindus worship as God. In the Buddha's teaching the admirable friend is a wise companion on the road, and each person still walks the path themselves.
neighbors.shared: find the friend who tells you the truth, either way.

neighbors.heading: repel it with something better
neighbors.text: Today a guest mocked the host in front of everyone, and Yudhishthira went after him with gentle words instead of guards. Muslims hear this in the Qur'an: "Repel the evil deed with one which is better," and an old enemy may become a close friend. Another verse says that when the foolish speak to God's servants, they answer: "Peace."
neighbors.difference: The epic lets two answers stand side by side: Yudhishthira's gentleness and Bhishma's firmness. The Qur'an names the better answer as God's way for believers, with God's reward, while still allowing wrongs to be resisted.
neighbors.shared: a gentle sentence can keep a guest at the table.

neighbors.heading: kindness that can't be beaten
neighbors.text: Today the host answered an insult with a gentle word, while the elder answered with steel. The Stoic emperor Marcus Aurelius wrote that a genuine kind disposition is invincible: what can even the most violent person do to you, if you stay kind and, when there's a chance, gently set them right? He meant it as daily practice.
neighbors.difference: For Marcus, kindness is reason at work, owed to every person as part of one human community. In the epic, Yudhishthira's gentleness is a host's dharma, and the poem gives Bhishma's sharper answer room too.
neighbors.shared: the first answer to an insult can still be kind.

neighbors.heading: every heart a jewel
neighbors.text: Today a guest fell into a pool, his host's brother laughed, and the hurt grew toward a war. Sikh scripture keeps a warning for that moment. Sheikh Farid's lines say: don't speak even one harsh word, for the True Lord lives in everyone; don't break anyone's heart, because every heart is a priceless jewel.
neighbors.difference: The epic shows the laugh and lets its harm unfold for years, without excusing what Duryodhana does next. Farid grounds the rule in God: wounding a heart wounds the place where the True Lord lives.
neighbors.shared: a laugh at someone's fall can outlast the fall.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1384, Salok of Sheikh Farid (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: restore, don't mock
neighbors.text: Today a man walked into a pool he took for floor, and the laughter behind him became a grudge. Paul wrote about moments like that: "if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted." Help first. You might slip next.
neighbors.difference: Duryodhana's slip is only a mistake about a floor, and Yudhishthira does send dry clothes. Paul is speaking of moral failings among believers: be gentle, because everyone needs God's mercy.
neighbors.shared: the one who slipped today could be you tomorrow.

neighbors.heading: not without giving first
neighbors.text: Today Draupadi served the guests, then her husbands, and ate last, and the sun's vessel kept the forest camp fed. Buddhists keep a saying of the Buddha close to this: if people knew, as he knew, the fruit of giving and sharing, they would not eat without first giving, even if it were their last mouthful.
neighbors.difference: Draupadi's serving keeps a household's duty to its guests, and a god's gift turns on it. For the Buddha, giving trains the giver's own mind, loosening stinginess on the way to freedom.
neighbors.shared: a table feels fuller when someone eats last on purpose.

neighbors.heading: servant of all
neighbors.text: Today Draupadi fed everyone before herself, in a camp that owned nothing. Jesus told his friends that greatness runs the other way: "whosoever will be first among you, shall be the servant of all." Popes have long used a title with the same idea in it: servant of the servants of God.
neighbors.difference: Draupadi serves as the heart of a household keeping the guest-duty of dharma. For Catholics, serving last follows Christ, who said he came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life.
neighbors.shared: the one who serves last holds the whole table together.
neighbors.sources: Mark 10:44 (Douay-Rheims) · Mark 10:45 (paraphrase) · the papal title Servus servorum Dei (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the right time to be angry
neighbors.text: Today a married couple argued in the forest: Draupadi said now is the time for strength; Yudhishthira called forgiveness the strength of the strong. Aristotle saw the same knot. Anyone can get angry, he wrote; that's easy. But to be angry with the right person, to the right degree, at the right time, for the right reason and in the right way is hard.
neighbors.difference: Aristotle looks for a middle way, set by reason and good habits. Draupadi and Yudhishthira argue from dharma and old stories of Prahlada and Bali, and the epic leaves both of them standing.
neighbors.shared: the hard part isn't choosing strength or mercy; it's knowing when.

neighbors.heading: a season for everything
neighbors.text: Today Draupadi quoted Prahlada: don't forgive always, don't use force always; there's a time for each. Jews read the same wisdom in Ecclesiastes: "To every thing there is a season," it begins, with "a time to keep silence, and a time to speak," and "a time of war, and a time of peace." Ashkenazi custom reads the book on Sukkot.
neighbors.difference: Prahlada gives a king practical advice: learn to judge which time it is. Ecclesiastes is a poem about seasons people can't always control, and it ends by urging reverence for God.
neighbors.shared: mercy and strength each have their hour; wisdom is telling which.

neighbors.heading: whither thou goest
neighbors.text: Today Damayanti shared her one cloth with Nala and told him she wouldn't leave. Christians read the same stubborn love in Ruth, who refused to leave her mother-in-law: "whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge." Matthew's Gospel names Ruth in Jesus's family line.
neighbors.difference: Damayanti stays with a husband who, that same night, leaves her sleeping. Ruth's loyalty is to Naomi, her mother-in-law, and she takes Naomi's people and God as her own. Ruth is a book Christians share with Jews.
neighbors.shared: love often looks like refusing to take the road away.

neighbors.heading: love and mercy between you
neighbors.text: Today Damayanti wrapped her husband in half her only garment and refused the road home without him. Muslims read marriage this way in the Qur'an: God "created for you helpmeets from yourselves that ye might find rest in them, and He ordained between you love and mercy." Muslims also remember Khadijah, the Prophet's first wife, who stood by him when others didn't.
neighbors.difference: The epic tests Damayanti's faithfulness to the breaking point, and Nala, not in his right mind, leaves. The Qur'an calls the love and mercy of marriage one of God's signs, a gift God places between two people.
neighbors.shared: notice who stays beside you when there's only one cloth left.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 30:21 (Pickthall 1930) · Khadijah in the hadith and the Prophet's biography (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: what God hath joined
neighbors.text: Today Savitri learned her chosen husband would die within a year, and said she would not choose twice. Catholics see marriage as a choice made once, too. Jesus said: "What therefore God hath joined together, let no man put asunder." The Church teaches that the bond of a sacramental marriage, once fully made, lasts until death.
neighbors.difference: Savitri chooses before any wedding, and her faithfulness follows Satyavan to Death himself. In Catholic teaching the bond holds until death and then ends; a widow may marry again, and hope rests in God.
neighbors.shared: some choices are made once, and then kept.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 19:6 (Douay-Rheims) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1640 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: one light in two bodies
neighbors.text: Today Savitri said she had chosen once and wouldn't choose twice, even knowing the year ahead. Sikhs hold marriage that close. Guru Amar Das wrote that those who only sit together aren't truly husband and wife; husband and wife are one light in two bodies. In the Anand Karaj, a couple walks four rounds around the Guru Granth Sahib.
neighbors.difference: Savitri's choice is a promise kept against a known death, and later she argues her husband back from Yama. In the Sikh wedding, the four rounds join the couple to each other and to God, on one spiritual journey.
neighbors.shared: a choice of the heart is a promise already made.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 788, Guru Amar Das (paraphrase) · the Lavan, Ang 773–774, Guru Ram Das (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: who is rich?
neighbors.text: Today a prince in exile said the happy person cooks simple greens at home and owes nothing. The rabbis asked a twin question: who is rich? Ben Zoma answered, the one who rejoices in his portion, and quoted a psalm: "thou shalt eat the labour of thine hands: happy shalt thou be."
neighbors.difference: Yudhishthira's happy person has outer conditions: a home, no debts, no exile. Ben Zoma's riches are inward: gladness in whatever portion you have, wherever you are.
neighbors.shared: a simple supper can be a whole happiness.

neighbors.heading: the best riches
neighbors.text: Today the yaksha asked who is happy, and the answer was small: greens at home, nothing owed. Buddhists keep a verse that points the same way: "Health is the greatest of gifts, contentedness the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvana the highest happiness." Contentment, here, is counted as wealth.
neighbors.difference: Yudhishthira's happiness is a householder's: a home, a supper, nothing owed. The Dhammapada honors contentment too, but names nirvana as the highest happiness, a freedom beyond any home, and Buddhist monks and nuns leave home to seek it.
neighbors.shared: enough, held gladly, is already a kind of wealth.

neighbors.heading: be fair among your children
neighbors.text: Today Yudhishthira chose to save Madri's son, not his strongest brother, so both mothers would have a living son. Muslims carry a hadith about fairness at home. When a father gave one son a gift, the Prophet asked whether he had given the same to all his children. He hadn't. The Prophet said: fear God, and be just among your children.
neighbors.difference: Yudhishthira's fairness is a life-or-death choice between two mothers' lines. The hadith is about everyday gifts from a parent, and it places fairness under God's watch.
neighbors.shared: fairness at home is a kind of love everyone can see.

neighbors.heading: choosing against your own side
neighbors.text: Today Yudhishthira, Kunti's son, chose to bring back Madri's son, so the family would stay fair. Philosophers test fairness this way too. John Rawls asked people to design society's rules as if they didn't know which place in it they would end up in. Choose from there, he argued, and you'll choose fairly.
neighbors.difference: Rawls asks us to imagine forgetting where we stand. Yudhishthira knows exactly where he stands, Kunti's living son, and chooses against his own side anyway, out of dharma and loyalty to both mothers.
neighbors.shared: fairness sometimes means choosing what isn't best for your side.
neighbors.sources: John Rawls, A Theory of Justice, the veil of ignorance (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Udyoga: the embassy, Krishna's counsel, Karna and Kunti

neighbors.heading: the carpenter's bread
neighbors.text: Today Krishna turned down a prince's feast and ate in Vidura's plain house. Sikhs tell a story that sounds very close. Guru Nanak, tradition says, refused the banquet of a rich official, Malik Bhago, and ate the coarse bread of Bhai Lalo, a carpenter. Squeezed in the Guru's hand, Lalo's bread gave milk; Bhago's, blood.
neighbors.difference: Krishna's reason is love: he won't eat where there is neither love nor need. Guru Nanak's is honesty: bread earned by hard work, set beside bread squeezed from the poor.
neighbors.shared: where you choose to eat can say more than a speech.
neighbors.sources: Janamsakhi tradition of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: I must abide at thy house
neighbors.text: Today Krishna passed by the prince's feast and stayed under Vidura's plain roof. Jesus made a choice like that too. In Jericho, with a crowd around him, he looked up into a tree and said: "Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house." The crowd murmured. The visit changed Zacchaeus.
neighbors.difference: Krishna refuses the table of a man who means harm. Jesus chooses the table of a man the crowd calls a sinner, and the visit becomes the way back: Zacchaeus gives half his goods to the poor.
neighbors.shared: a shared meal can be the start of a changed life.

items.lessonTitle: Bhishma Parva (the Gita re-read in place, 6 sessions)

neighbors.heading: going for refuge
neighbors.text: Today Arjuna put down his bow and said: I am your disciple; teach me; I come to you for refuge. Buddhists know that word well. The Three Refuges begin "Buddham saranam gacchami," I go for refuge to the Buddha, and then to the Dhamma, his teaching, and to the Sangha, the community.
neighbors.difference: Arjuna takes refuge in Krishna, his friend and charioteer, whom he comes to see as God. Buddhists take refuge in the Buddha as the teacher who found the way and showed it, in his teaching, and in each other.
neighbors.shared: admitting you need a teacher can be the bravest moment.
neighbors.sources: Khuddakapatha 1, the Three Refuges (Pali; English paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: lord, teach us
neighbors.text: Today a warrior between two armies stopped fighting and became a student: I am your disciple, teach me. Catholics remember a quieter version of that moment. After watching Jesus pray, one of his disciples asked: "Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples." Jesus answered with the Our Father.
neighbors.difference: Arjuna asks what to do with a terrible duty, and hears a teaching about the self that cannot be killed. The disciples ask how to pray, and Jesus gives them words to say together to God as Father.
neighbors.shared: a real teaching often starts with someone brave enough to ask.

neighbors.heading: peace has to be made
neighbors.text: Today Bhishma, lying on his bed of arrows, asked Duryodhana to let the war end with him, and was turned down. Philosophers have wrestled with refusals like that. Immanuel Kant wrote that peace between neighbors isn't the natural state of things; it has to be established, on purpose, by people who choose it and build it.
neighbors.difference: Bhishma's plea is a dying elder's word to his own family, inside dharma. Kant was thinking of nations, and of laws and agreements strong enough to hold even when people don't feel peaceful.
neighbors.shared: peace doesn't just happen; someone has to ask for it.
neighbors.sources: Immanuel Kant, Perpetual Peace (1795), second section (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: seek peace, and pursue it
neighbors.text: Today a dying man used his last strength to plead for peace between cousins. Jews pray a psalm that asks the same: "seek peace, and pursue it." Hillel taught: be among the disciples of Aaron, loving peace and pursuing peace, loving people and bringing them near to the Torah. Pursue means you don't wait for it. You go after it.
neighbors.difference: Bhishma's plea comes at the end, from a bed of arrows, after a war he fought in. Hillel asks people to chase peace every day, in small quarrels, long before anyone picks up a weapon.
neighbors.shared: it's never wrong to ask for peace, even late.
neighbors.sources: Psalm 34:15 (JPS 1917; 34:14 in many English Bibles) · Pirkei Avot 1:12 (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Karna: the wheel stuck, the death

neighbors.heading: the midwives' answer
neighbors.text: Today Krishna told of a man who spoke the truth to robbers, and travelers died for it. Christians wrestle with this knot too. In Exodus, the Hebrew midwives disobey Pharaoh's order to kill baby boys and give him an evasive answer, and the text says: "Therefore God dealt well with the midwives." Augustine still taught that every lie is wrong.
neighbors.difference: Krishna weighs truth by what it does to living beings. Many Christians, following Augustine, hold that a lie is never right, even to save a life, and praise the midwives' mercy rather than their words; others read it differently.
neighbors.shared: truth and kindness are meant to walk together.

neighbors.heading: not a liar who makes peace
neighbors.text: Today Krishna told Arjuna that truth is weighed by what it does to living beings. Muslims hold truthfulness close, and a hadith names a narrow exception that sounds like this: the one who makes peace between people, passing on good words to bring them together, is not a liar.
neighbors.difference: Krishna's teaching is broad: weigh each truth by its effect. In Islam truthfulness is the rule, scholars allow only a few named exceptions such as reconciling people, and many prefer gentle, indirect words to an outright falsehood.
neighbors.shared: honest words are meant to bring people back together.

items.lessonTitle: Shalya: Duryodhana in the lake, the mace fight

neighbors.heading: this day, in paradise
neighbors.text: Today Kripa told a beaten king it wasn't too late for peace, and Duryodhana said no. Catholics treasure a moment when someone said yes at the very end. On the cross, a thief asked Jesus to remember him, and Jesus answered: "Amen I say to thee, this day thou shalt be with me in paradise."
neighbors.difference: Kripa offers peace between cousins and a share of a kingdom; Duryodhana refuses out of loyalty to friends who died. The thief asks for God's mercy, which Catholics teach stays open until the last breath.
neighbors.shared: it isn't too late while you can still ask.

neighbors.heading: the shining bronze
neighbors.text: Today an old teacher told Duryodhana there was still time, and he turned it down. Sikhs tell of a man who turned. Sajjan, tradition says, welcomed travelers by day and robbed them by night. Guru Nanak sang to him of bronze that shines but shows black when it's rubbed. Sajjan heard himself in it, and changed his life.
neighbors.difference: Duryodhana hears plain counsel and refuses, out of loyalty to the dead. In the Sikh story, change comes through the Guru's song, heard by a man in his own house, and an honest life follows.
neighbors.shared: a true word, heard at the right moment, can turn a life.
neighbors.sources: Janamsakhi tradition of Sajjan (paraphrase) · Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 729, Suhi, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

items.lessonTitle: Shalya: Duryodhana in the lake, the mace fight

neighbors.heading: my creatures are drowning
neighbors.text: Today the war was won, and Yudhishthira told Bhima to take his foot off a fallen king. Jewish tradition holds the same line. Proverbs says: "Rejoice not when thine enemy falleth." And the rabbis tell that when the angels wanted to sing as the Egyptians drowned, God stopped them: my creatures are drowning, and you sing?
neighbors.difference: In the epic the winners stand downcast while flowers fall on the loser, and the argument stays open. In the rabbis' story God grieves for the enemy, and Israel's rescue is still celebrated.
neighbors.shared: even a just win leaves room for grief.

neighbors.heading: victory breeds hatred
neighbors.text: Today the winners of a war couldn't agree how to treat the loser, and flowers fell on the fallen king. Buddhists keep a verse for a field like that: "Victory breeds hatred, for the conquered is unhappy. He who has given up both victory and defeat, he, the contented, is happy."
neighbors.difference: The epic weighs the victory: what was done, why, and what it cost, and lets every side speak. The Dhammapada steps outside the contest, pointing to a peace beyond winning and losing.
neighbors.shared: the one on the ground is still someone's family.

neighbors.heading: a stranger, a traveler
neighbors.text: Today Vidura told a grieving king about a man in a well, still reaching for the honey. Muslims keep a short saying of the Prophet with the same clear eyes: be in this world as if you were a stranger, or a traveler passing through. And the Qur'an calls the life of this world a passing comfort that can deceive.
neighbors.difference: Vidura's story describes everyone, gently, to comfort a king in grief. The hadith is advice for living: hold the world lightly, because the traveler is on the way home to God.
neighbors.shared: time is short, so hold the sweet things gently.

neighbors.heading: the honey in the well
neighbors.text: Today a man hung in a well between a serpent and an elephant, licking honey. Leo Tolstoy found the same parable, which he called an Eastern fable, in his own crisis. In A Confession he pictured himself on that branch, and wrote that the honey no longer tasted sweet. It sent him searching for what makes a life mean something.
neighbors.difference: Vidura uses the story to console a king: everyone hangs there, so don't be swept away by grief. Tolstoy used it as a mirror for his own despair, and spent years looking for an answer.
neighbors.shared: honest about time, and still able to taste the honey.

items.lessonTitle: Shanti and Anushasana: Bhishma's teachings from the bed of arrows (selections)

neighbors.heading: water for every soldier
neighbors.text: Today a pigeon made a fire for the hunter who had caged his mate. Sikhs tell of Bhai Kanhaiya, who carried water across a battlefield to wounded soldiers of both sides. Accused of helping the enemy, he said he saw no enemy, only the Guru's light in every face. Guru Gobind Singh, tradition says, gave him ointment for their wounds too.
neighbors.difference: The pigeon's story shows hospitality to a guest at your door, told to the extreme. Bhai Kanhaiya's service is on a battlefield, healing, because the Guru taught him to see God in everyone.
neighbors.shared: a guest is a guest, even the one who hurt you.

neighbors.heading: if thine enemy hunger
neighbors.text: Today a pigeon warmed and fed the hunter who had caught his mate, and the hunter laid down his nets. Christians hear Paul in it: "if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head." Then: "overcome evil with good."
neighbors.difference: The pigeon's gift is the duty to a guest, told to the extreme, and the hunter is transformed. Paul's teaching rests on Jesus's command to love enemies, and leaves judgment to God.
neighbors.shared: kindness to the one who hurt you can change them.

neighbors.heading: the widow's two coins
neighbors.text: Today a mongoose said a royal sacrifice wasn't worth a poor family's handful of barley. Jesus said something close at the Temple. Watching rich people put in large sums, he saw a poor widow drop in two small coins, and said: "Amen I say to you, this poor widow hath cast in more than all they who have cast into the treasury."
neighbors.difference: In the epic, the poor family gives every portion to a guest who turns out to be Dharma, and they are carried to heaven. Jesus simply notices the widow; the Gospel tells no reward, only his words.
neighbors.shared: the size of a gift isn't measured in coins.

neighbors.heading: a little, worth a thousand
neighbors.text: Today a half-golden mongoose rolled in a king's grand sacrifice and found it lighter than a poor family's barley. Buddhists keep a verse spoken before the Buddha with the same surprise: some give from the little they have, and a gift given from little is worth a thousand times as much.
neighbors.difference: In the epic, Dharma himself comes as the guest and rewards the family with heaven. Buddhist teaching looks to the giver's mind: a gift from little, given gladly, shapes the giver, whatever comes of it.
neighbors.shared: a small gift given fully can outweigh a great show.

items.lessonTitle: the Pandavas' last journey, Yudhishthira's dog, heaven

neighbors.heading: can they suffer?
neighbors.text: Today Indra told Yudhishthira the dog didn't count, and he would rather give up heaven than leave it. The philosopher Jeremy Bentham asked who counts, too. Of animals he wrote: "The question is not, Can they reason? nor, Can they talk? but, Can they suffer?" A creature that can't repay you is still owed care.
neighbors.difference: Yudhishthira's answer is about faithfulness: he won't abandon one who is devoted to him and has nowhere else to go. Bentham's is about suffering: any creature that can feel pain counts, devoted or not.
neighbors.shared: the smallest one on the road still counts.
neighbors.sources: Jeremy Bentham, An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation (1789), chapter 17, footnote

neighbors.heading: the shepherd and the young goat
neighbors.text: Today a king refused heaven rather than leave behind a dog. Jews tell of care for animals too. Proverbs says: "A righteous man regardeth the life of his beast." And a midrash says Moses chased a runaway young goat to a spring, carried it back on his shoulders, and God said: this is who will shepherd my people.
neighbors.difference: Yudhishthira's test is about loyalty: refusing to turn away a creature devoted to him. In the midrash, Moses's care for a young goat shows he is fit to lead people, and Jewish law forbids causing animals needless pain.
neighbors.shared: the way you treat the smallest shows who you are.
